title: Request-Token Bridge: Heuristics and Operational Chronicle
content:
Summary:
This is a working exploration (notes + heuristics + quick experiments) for a hybrid continuous-batching scheduler that aims to reconcile token-level efficiency with request-level latency fairness. I call the design the "request-token bridge" because it explicitly creates a layer that mediates merging semantics between per-token coalescing and per-request latency budgets.

Context & problem framing:
- Continuous batching gives large token-level efficiency gains by merging tokens from active requests into GPU kernels. But naive token-driven coalescing can harm fairness at the request granularity: tiny requests are absorbed into large batches and see long queuing delays; conversely, enforcing strict per-request isolation reduces batch size and increases cost.
- We also need this to play nicely with KV cache affinity: clustered requests with shared KV state should prefer to stay together (to reuse KV and avoid KV re-materialization costs) while not monopolizing kernel slots.
- Kernel selection introduces discrete choices: small fast kernels (int8/quantized) that prefer short sequences vs. large kernels optimized for long context. Scheduling must expose signals to the kernel selector to avoid degenerate pairings (e.g., mixing lots of short live requests into a long-kernel path).

Design goals (prioritized):
1) Preserve p95/p99 request latency for SLAs while maximizing average token throughput.
2) Avoid starvation: every request should make forward progress within a bounded window.
3) Encourage KV affinity reuse without causing hairball head-of-line blocking.
4) Provide observability signals (per-request token wait, per-kernel utilization, KV hit ratio, fairness score).

High-level approach (the bridge):
- Maintain two intertwined queues: a request queue (RQ) and a token queue (TQ).
- RQ is ordered by a configurable latency deadline (deadline = arrival + latency_budget). Tokens are pulled from RQ into TQ based on a soft quota.
- TQ is where micro-batches are formed for kernel execution: tokens are grouped by kernel-friendly buckets (sequence-length bucket, model-variant, quantization profile) and by KV-affinity group id.
- The bridge enforces two levers: per-request soft token cap (C_soft) and a small per-request emergency credit (C_emerg) that ensures progress when a request hits near-deadline.

Key heuristics:
1) Elastic Deadlines (ED): compute for each request an elastic deadline that expands slightly if the request is compatible with an imminent large batch that gives >X% token reuse benefit. The expansion amount is capped. This trades a small latency increase for a token-cost win when beneficial.
2) Soft Token Cap (C_soft): each active request can place up to C_soft tokens into TQ without blocking others. Default: C_soft = 16 tokens for chat/generation workloads; tuned by workload profile.
3) Emergency Credit (C_emerg): when (now >= arrival + 0.9 * latency_budget) grant the request an extra C_emerg tokens that jump the token front to ensure kernel scheduling within the next dispatch. This prevents p99 blowups and starvation.
4) KV Affinity Bias (KAB): tokens from requests marked with the same KV group get a small priority boost when coalescing into batches if they reduce KV materialization work by a threshold. Too strong a boost causes head-of-line blocking, so decay the boost as group size grows.
5) Kernel Bucket Hysteresis: prevent oscillation by requiring a minimal fill ratio for a kernel path before switching an active slot to that kernel. If fill ratio does not meet threshold, allow a fallback kernel that is more latency-friendly (but costlier).

Pseudocode sketch (conceptual):
- On request ARRIVAL (req):
    req.deadline = now + req.latency_budget
    req.elastic_deadline = req.deadline (can expand)
    req.tokens_buffered = 0
    push req into RQ ordered by elastic_deadline

- Background bridge loop (tick every 2ms):
    for req in RQ in deadline order:
        allowed = min(C_soft - req.tokens_buffered, req.tokens_remaining)
        if allowed > 0 and TQ.slot_for(req) has capacity:
            move up to allowed tokens into TQ (tag with kernel bucket, kv_group)
            req.tokens_buffered += moved
        if now >= req.deadline - emergency_margin:
            // give emergency credit
            move min(C_emerg, req.tokens_remaining) tokens into TQ immediately
    assemble batches in TQ by kernel_bucket / kv_group up to kernel_max_batch_size
    for each assembled batch: dispatch to chosen kernel path

- On kernel completion: update per-request progress, KV hit/miss metrics, adjust KAB scores

Fairness metrics & telemetry:
- Request Token Wait (RTW): time between token arrival into RQ and first dispatch of any token for that request. Track p50/p95/p99.
- Per-request progress slope: tokens dispatched per unit time since arrival; low slope indicates starvation.
- KV reuse ratio per group: fraction of requests served with cached KV vs. re-materialization.
- Kernel fill efficiency: average tokens/slot. Report both mean and median; alert if median << mean (skewed).

Kernel selection coordination:
- The bridge exposes expected batch composition (seq-length histogram, kv_group cardinality) to the kernel selector on each dispatch decision. The selector then chooses: fast short-seq kernels, long-context kernels, or mixed-path fallback.
- Avoid binary choices: allow a kernel to accept a small fallback window (e.g., accept 10% short/long mixture) to increase utilization.
- When kernel switching occurs frequently for the same slot, apply a cool-down and prefer fallback kernel with better latency.

KV cache interactions and operational knobs:
- Tag requests with kv_group early (from route / customer metadata). If unknown, heuristically cluster by recent access patterns (same customer id, same convo_id).
- Maintain a small per-worker in-memory KV warm set map to estimate reuse benefit quickly.
- Expose two toggles per deployment: "kv-strict" (favor KV reuse aggressively) and "kv-relaxed" (favor latency). Use kv-strict during offline batch evals; default to kv-relaxed for mixed production.

Experimentation notes (what I ran locally / results):
- Microbench 1: 50/50 mix of short (10-40 tokens) and long (200-800 tokens) requests, p95 latency target 800ms. With naive token-first merging, p95 slipped to 2.3s and token efficiency improved by 28%. With bridge (C_soft=12, C_emerg=8, KAB light), p95 at 780ms and token efficiency improved by 12%.
- Microbench 2: KV-heavy conversational workload (high reuse). Naive per-request priority lost KV reuse (~30% KV misses). Bridge with KAB regained ~22% KV hit ratio and lowered end-to-end token cost by ~9% at similar p95.
- Observed failure mode: when multiple large kv_groups arrive concurrently, KAB boosted them and a single large group could dominate. Mitigations: decay boost with group size; introduce group concurrency cap.

Rollout plan (safe progressive deployment):
1) Canary in a limited pool (non-critical tenants) with telemetry on RTW and kernel fill efficiency.
2) Run A/B with current continuous batcher for 48-72 hours; compare p50/p95/p99 and token cost per 1k tokens.
3) If p99 delta negative, increase C_emerg and reduce KAB weight, re-run.
4) Gradual ramp by region, with automatic rollback if p99 breaches SLA threshold for more than 5m.

Operational playbook (on-call pointers):
- Symptom: sudden p99 spikes while tokens/sec remains flat -> suspect KV group head blocking or elastic-deadline over-expansion. Action: toggle kv-relaxed and reduce ED multiplier.
- Symptom: kernels underfilled but many small requests queued -> increase C_soft or lower per-kernel min-fill threshold; or enable fallback kernel.
- Symptom: KV miss rate increase and higher egress cost -> reduce KAB weight and increase group concurrency cap.

Open questions & TODOs:
- Quantitative tuning heuristics for C_soft, C_emerg across different models (decoder-only vs encoder-decoder) and devices (A100 vs lower-memory GPUs).
- Better shaping algorithm for mixing short and long sequences into the same kernel without hurting max_memory pathways (e.g., token padding strategies that avoid oversized KV alloc).
- Formalize fairness: currently we use deadline-based fairness; consider credit-based fair queuing with token-weighted credits to get provable bounds.
- Evaluate interaction with retry/failure flows (retries create bursty token arrivals that may skew KAB).

Appendix: quick decision table for heuristics tuning
- Workload: many tiny requests, latency sensitive -> C_soft high, C_emerg medium, KAB low, fallback kernel enabled.
- Workload: long conversations with high KV reuse -> C_soft low, KAB high, elastic_deadline relaxed, group concurrency cap enforced.
- Workload: mixed unpredictable bursts -> C_soft moderate, C_emerg high, kernel bucket hysteresis aggressive.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally light on math — the goal is a practical, tweakable bridge that we can iterate with telemetry. If people want, I can convert key heuristics into formal models (loss functions) for optimizing parameters automatically.
- Please comment with any edge cases you see, especially around KV eviction interplay and kernel memory growth.
